row.basis: Joseph's prison cupbearer dream; grapes pressed into Pharaoh's cup
row.note: The commentary's imprisoned cupbearer dreams of pressing grapes and serving wine; Genesis gives the same prison dream in which the cupbearer squeezes grapes into Pharaoh's cup, a direct scene parallel.

row.basis: Cupbearer forgets Joseph
row.note: The commentary says the cupbearer forgets Joseph after his release, leaving Joseph in prison; Genesis likewise says the restored cupbearer did not remember Joseph, making the delay part of the shared story.

row.basis: Two-year delay before Pharaoh's dreams
row.note: The commentary makes delayed recollection lengthen Joseph's imprisonment; Genesis marks two full years before Pharaoh dreams and the cupbearer remembers, giving that wait a measured duration.

row.basis: Cupbearer recalls his failure
row.note: The commentary's freed cupbearer remembers Joseph only after a long interval; Genesis has him recall his failure before Pharaoh and recount Joseph's prison interpretation, ending the forgotten interval.

row.basis: Surplus stored in the cities
row.note: The commentary links Joseph's seven abundant years with preserving grain for scarcity; Genesis says Joseph gathers the produce of those years and stores food in the cities, the same plan of holding yield through time.

row.basis: End of the years of plenty
row.note: The commentary orders Joseph's story as abundance, hard years, then renewed yield; Genesis says the seven years of plenty end, marking the same turn in the agricultural calendar.

row.basis: Famine follows abundance
row.note: The commentary's stored grain is for the years of hardship; Genesis says famine begins and the land still has food in Egypt, showing the preserved yield surviving the time of loss.

row.basis: Stored grain released beyond Egypt
row.note: The commentary's final Joseph year restores productive pressing after scarcity; Genesis has all lands come to Egypt to buy grain, showing stored abundance flowing outward when famine arrives.

row.basis: Oath and exclusion from the sworn land
row.note: The commentary places an oath just before a verdict of loss; Numbers says the rebellious generation will not see the land sworn to their ancestors, joining oath, missed inheritance, and a closed future.

row.basis: Caleb as the exception
row.note: After the generation is excluded, Numbers singles out Caleb, who followed fully and will enter the land; this gives a precise biblical instance of a general loss followed by an exception for the faithful.

row.basis: A thousand years as a day and night watch
row.note: The commentary holds a long era and a short day-part together; the psalm measures a thousand years as yesterday or a night watch, explicitly collapsing vast time into a brief interval.

row.basis: Morning growth fades by evening
row.note: The commentary hears the afternoon as a closing day with dwindling light and a life nearing its end; the psalm describes grass flourishing in the morning and fading by evening, making mortality visible in the daily cycle.

row.basis: Seventy or eighty years pass quickly
row.note: The commentary says the same word can name an era and a person's age; the psalm measures human years at seventy or eighty and says they soon fly, linking a long life to a finite span.

row.basis: Oath that bars entry into rest
row.note: The commentary's opening oath stands at the threshold of a verdict; the psalm ends its warning with God's sworn denial of entry into rest, a close formal and thematic parallel of oath followed by loss.

row.basis: Merchants impatient for the sacred day to end
row.note: The commentary makes the day's closing edge a time when work and opportunity run short; Amos depicts grain sellers asking when the new moon and Sabbath will end so they can trade and falsify measures, turning sacred time into an obstacle to profit.

row.basis: An oath against those who exploit the poor
row.note: The commentary's garden owners swear to keep the poor from their harvest; Amos has the Lord swear not to forget merchants who trample the needy, joining oath, withheld food, and judgment.

row.basis: Grapes left for the poor
row.note: The commentary's garden owners plan to exclude the poor from their crop; Deuteronomy commands leaving remaining grapes for the stranger, orphan, and widow, setting shared yield against total retention.

row.basis: Withheld grain curses its owner
row.note: The commentary contrasts a hand that keeps produce with one that lets its extract become a gift; Proverbs says people curse the one who withholds grain and bless the seller, making the ethical difference between retention and release explicit.

row.basis: Work while it is day
row.note: The commentary hears afternoon as the closing part of the day, when undone work has little time left; Jesus says to do the work while it is day because night comes when no one can work, making the shrinking window explicit.

row.basis: Pressed measure overflowing as a gift
row.note: The commentary makes pressing yield an image of generosity when the extract flows out; Jesus describes a measure pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing into another's lap, a striking image of abundance given away.

row.basis: A thirsty tongue with no available sip
row.note: The commentary's dried tongue and failed rescue-sip image meets the rich man after death asking for a drop of water to cool his tongue; Luke makes relief unavailable after the decisive time has passed.

row.basis: Fortunes reversed after death
row.note: The commentary's withheld garden yield ends in deprivation; Abraham tells the rich man that he received good things in life while Lazarus received bad, but their conditions are now reversed, making the lost opportunity irreversible.

row.basis: Full wage for the eleventh-hour workers
row.note: The commentary's closing hour warns that little time remains to finish work; Jesus' parable pays those hired at the eleventh hour a full denarius, countering the assumption that a late start must mean a diminished share.

row.basis: Honi sleeps through seventy years
row.note: The commentary links refuge in a cave with sleep that seems brief to the sleepers but spans centuries; Honi sleeps within a rocky shelter for seventy years and wakes into a changed generation, a Jewish time-dislocation parallel.

row.ref: Gregory of Tours, Glory of the Martyrs 1.95
row.basis: The Seven Sleepers of Ephesus
row.note: The commentary's cave youths sleep through centuries and wake in a changed age; Gregory recounts the Christian Seven Sleepers of Ephesus in their cave, a direct narrative parallel whose chronology varies among tellings.

row.basis: Hebrews repeats the oath of exclusion
row.note: The commentary frames the oath as the threshold to a verdict of loss; Hebrews quotes Psalm 95's oath that the wilderness generation will not enter God's rest, reading the oath as a warning about salvation and missed time.

row.basis: Believers enter the promised rest
row.note: The commentary moves from loss to an exception for believers; Hebrews interprets the wilderness oath by saying that those who believe enter the rest, giving faith the role of escape from the exclusion.

row.basis: Midrash explains Joseph's extra prison years
row.note: The commentary treats the cupbearer's forgetting as a long delay; Genesis Rabbah reads Joseph's doubled plea to be remembered as the reason for two more years in prison, turning the delay into a lesson about reliance and trust.

row.basis: Human labor continues until evening
row.note: The commentary describes asr as the hour when work is nearly done and remaining time narrows; the psalm says people go out to work and labor until evening, giving that closing edge an ordinary workday scene.

row.basis: Prayer at evening, morning, and noon
row.note: The commentary pairs devotion at the day's two edges; the psalmist says he prays at evening, morning, and noon, extending the pattern into a full daily cycle.

row.basis: Praise in morning and night
row.note: The commentary hears the day's beginning and close together; the psalm appoints praise of steadfast love in the morning and faithfulness at night, a daily liturgical counterpart.

row.basis: Prayer as evening offering
row.note: The commentary names the afternoon prayer and the day's closing edge; the psalm asks that prayer rise like incense and raised hands like an evening offering, joining prayer to the late-day rite.

row.basis: Prayer times bounded by afternoon and evening
row.note: The commentary notes that asr can name the afternoon prayer; the Mishnah sets the afternoon prayer's time until evening, placing a daily prayer within the same shrinking daylight boundary.

row.basis: Isaac's evening meditation read as afternoon prayer
row.note: The commentary leaves open whether asr is the afternoon hour or a wider span of time; the Talmud derives the afternoon prayer from Isaac going out to meditate toward evening, giving that hour a Jewish interpretive tradition.

row.basis: Prayer at the ninth hour
row.note: The commentary includes the afternoon prayer among possible senses of asr; Acts places Peter and John at the temple at the ninth hour, the hour of prayer, showing a Christian practice at a named late-day hour.

row.basis: Alms and prayers remembered
row.note: The commentary describes the squeezed extract as generosity flowing outward; the angel tells Cornelius that his prayers and alms have risen as a memorial, linking devotional practice with concrete giving.

row.basis: Third, sixth, and ninth-hour prayer
row.note: The commentary names a fixed afternoon prayer within the day; Tertullian recognizes third, sixth, and ninth hours as customary times for prayer, showing a Christian daily rhythm that includes the closing daylight hours.

row.basis: Daily offerings at morning and twilight
row.note: The commentary pairs the day's edges and names the afternoon prayer; Exodus assigns one lamb to morning and another to twilight, a daily ritual cycle ending as daylight closes.

row.basis: Rain waters furrows and blesses growth
row.note: The commentary traces rain from squeezed clouds to grain and plants; the psalm describes God watering furrows with showers and blessing their growth, a close rain-to-crop sequence.

row.basis: The year crowned with abundance
row.note: The commentary lets asr name both a day-part and a long age, then links time to yield; the psalm says God crowns the year with goodness, joining a temporal cycle to its harvest.

row.basis: Rain fills threshing floors and vats
row.note: The commentary's squeezed-cloud image leads to grain, plants, and gardens; Joel describes threshing floors full of grain and vats overflowing after rain, a parallel chain from water to agricultural abundance.

row.basis: Winepress as judgment
row.note: The commentary's pressing can yield a gift or leave a dry remainder; Joel summons the sickle and treading of a full winepress as the nations' judgment, making the same harvest image destructive.

row.basis: The divine warrior treads the winepress alone
row.note: The commentary distinguishes the flowing extract from the dry residue; Isaiah pictures God treading the winepress until garments are stained with blood, a counter-image in which pressing signifies judgment rather than bounty.

row.basis: The earth's vintage cast into God's winepress
row.note: The commentary's grape pressing may stand for a good yield; Revelation gathers the earth's vintage and casts it into the winepress of divine wrath, giving the harvest image an apocalyptic judgment sense.

row.basis: Blood flows from the winepress
row.note: The commentary describes pressing as separating liquid from dry pulp; Revelation says blood flows from the trampled winepress, turning that flow into a measure of catastrophic judgment.

row.basis: A rich man counts on many years of stored goods
row.note: The commentary's garden owner has a final crop and an aging life; Luke's rich farmer stores abundant produce and assumes many years ahead, making stored yield a wager on future time.

row.basis: The future ends that night
row.note: The commentary's old orchard owner loses the one harvest on which he depends; God tells Luke's farmer his life is required that very night, making the end of time arrive before expected use of stored goods.

row.basis: A great wind kills the children in a collapsing house
row.note: The commentary's garden is destroyed by a whirlwind while its owner has weak descendants; Job reports a wind that collapses a house onto his children, a specific parallel of destructive wind and vulnerable offspring.

row.basis: A plant briefly shelters a distressed person
row.note: The commentary calls asr a refuge for the distressed; Jonah's plant grows to shade him from discomfort, giving shelter a temporary, living form that can soon be lost.

row.basis: God as refuge in trouble
row.note: The commentary calls the refuge a haven for a person in distress; the psalm names God as refuge and strength, a help in trouble, matching the concrete relation of shelter to pressure.

row.basis: Children have a refuge
row.note: The commentary says lineage can be a place of refuge; Proverbs says the children of one who fears the Lord have refuge, directly joining descent and protection.

row.basis: Faith as a protective shield
row.note: The commentary links refuge to armor that wraps and protects the body; Paul describes the shield of faith extinguishing flaming arrows, giving the protective covering an ethical and spiritual use.

row.basis: Testing produces endurance
row.note: The commentary describes time's pressure as extracting an essence and connects the surah's final patience to a bitter extract; James says tested faith produces endurance, a specific ethical parallel between trial and patient strength.

row.basis: The delayed bridegroom and sleeping waiters
row.note: The commentary includes late arrival and a sleep that may last only a moment; Matthew's bridegroom is delayed and the waiting women all grow sleepy and sleep, placing delay and sleep inside a story about readiness.

row.basis: The door closes before the late arrivals
row.note: The commentary warns that work left undone near day's end may run out of time; Matthew's late bridesmaids arrive after the door is shut, making delay a lost opportunity.

row.basis: Menstruation as a timed ritual boundary
row.note: The commentary's lexicon describes the first menstruating girl as held at home for protection; Leviticus assigns menstrual bleeding a seven-day impurity and contact rules, offering a distinct ritual reading of that timed threshold rather than confirming the commentary's protective etymology.

row.basis: Arabic ع ص ر / Hebrew עצר; table sound correspondence, unverified
row.note: The package table gives Hebrew עצר a festival-assembly sense; Leviticus marks the eighth day with a sacred assembly, a calendrical use alongside the commentary's afternoon prayer and day-boundary senses, without establishing cognacy.

row.basis: A day and a thousand years
row.note: The commentary holds the long age and short day-part together; Second Peter applies the psalm's thousand-years-as-a-day scale to the apparent delay of the Lord's coming, making divine and human time differ.

row.basis: Delay as time for repentance
row.note: The commentary includes the sense of a late arrival and the dwindling time left to act; Second Peter interprets apparent delay as patience that gives people time to repent, turning lateness into mercy.

row.basis: Life as a mist that appears briefly
row.note: The commentary lets asr range from a long era to a fleeting instant; James calls human life a mist that appears briefly and vanishes, a precise but less developed image of life's short span.

row.basis: Arabic ص ب ر / Hebrew צבר; table sound correspondence, unverified
row.note: The commentary links its final word ṣabr, patience, to a bitter tree extract and to waiting through lean years while grain is saved; Genesis says Joseph heaped grain in extraordinary quantity. The table's ص ب ر / צבר match is only an unverified sound correspondence, not proof of cognacy.

row.basis: Arabic ع ص ر / Hebrew עצר; table sound correspondence, unverified
row.note: The commentary gives the Arabic dictionary sense of al-ʿaṣr as holding or detaining; Manoah asks to detain his visitor while preparing food, using Hebrew עצר. The package table marks the sound match as a candidate only.

row.basis: Arabic ع ص ر / Hebrew עצר; table sound correspondence, unverified
row.note: The commentary includes late or slow arrival and the sense of being held back; the Shunammite tells her servant not to slow her journey to Elisha, using Hebrew עצר. This is a precise semantic echo but the table does not verify cognacy.

row.basis: Arabic ع ص ر / Hebrew עצר; table sound correspondence, unverified
row.note: The commentary connects holding tightly with refuge and protection; Aaron stands between the dead and living while the plague is stopped with Hebrew עצר, a protective restraint that echoes that image.

row.basis: Arabic ع ص ر / Hebrew עצר; table sound correspondence, unverified
row.note: The commentary links squeezed rain clouds to grain and plants; Deuteronomy uses Hebrew עצר for shutting the heavens so rain and crop fail, a relevant withholding sense, though the root match remains unverified.

row.basis: Arabic ع ص ر / Hebrew עצר; table sound correspondence, unverified
row.note: The commentary contrasts rain that flows from clouds with a dry, pressed remnant; Job says that when God holds back waters they dry up, and when he releases them they flood the land, a close semantic fit through the table's unverified sound correspondence.

row.basis: Arabic ع ص ر / Hebrew עצר; table sound correspondence, unverified
row.note: The commentary describes a young woman held at a reproductive threshold; Genesis says God had closed the wombs of Abimelech's household using Hebrew עצר, a specific withholding sense but not proof that the roots are cognate.

row.basis: Joseph asks the released cupbearer to remember him
row.note: The commentary notes Joseph's request to be remembered and the cupbearer's later forgetting; Genesis gives the request itself, asking the cupbearer to mention him to Pharaoh and bring him out of prison.

row.basis: Joseph confined in fetters
row.note: The commentary places Joseph's waiting in prison; the psalm retells his story as feet bound in fetters until the promised time, giving the confinement a bodily image.

row.basis: Joseph tested until his word comes true
row.note: The commentary arranges Joseph's prison years around delayed remembrance and eventual release; the psalm says the word of the Lord tested Joseph until what he had said came to pass, interpreting the delay as a trial.

row.basis: Seven years of abundance forecast
row.note: The commentary follows Joseph's reading of Pharaoh's dream as a calendar of plenty and scarcity; Genesis predicts seven years of great abundance throughout Egypt, specifying the productive span.

row.basis: Seven famine years follow
row.note: The commentary's Joseph narrative turns from years of yield to years of hardship; Genesis forecasts seven years of famine after the abundance, making the saved grain's time horizon explicit.

row.basis: The plenty is forgotten in famine
row.note: The commentary says the hard years consume what was stored; Genesis adds that the famine is so severe that the former plenty is no longer remembered, a sharper account of yield erased by loss.

row.basis: The land produces abundantly during the good years
row.note: The commentary follows the movement from productive years to preserved grain; Genesis says the land yields abundantly through the seven years, the harvest that makes Joseph's storage possible.

row.basis: Joseph opens the storehouses in famine
row.note: The commentary ends Joseph's cycle with renewed access to produce after scarcity; Genesis says Joseph opens the storehouses and sells grain during the famine, showing reserve released when need arrives.

row.basis: Those who trample the needy
row.note: The commentary's garden owners plan to keep the poor from their crop; Amos addresses people who trample the needy and bring the poor to an end, naming the injustice that the garden scene dramatizes.

row.basis: Poor people traded for silver while wheat is sold
row.note: The commentary contrasts hoarded produce with giving; Amos condemns buyers who acquire the poor for silver and sell even wheat refuse, making grain control an instrument of exploitation.

row.basis: Do not close the hand against the poor
row.note: The commentary describes holding a gift back and excluding the poor from a garden; Deuteronomy forbids hardening the heart or shutting the hand against a poor kinsman, a direct ethical counterpoint.

row.basis: Open the hand to meet another's need
row.note: The commentary says squeezing can let its extract flow as generosity; Deuteronomy commands opening the hand and lending enough for the poor person's need, making release the ethical response to scarcity.

row.basis: Give freely without a grudging heart
row.note: The commentary contrasts a generous person with one who withholds or reclaims a gift; Deuteronomy commands giving without regret and promises blessing for the work, joining openhandedness to fruitful outcome.

row.basis: A forgotten sheaf left for the poor
row.note: The commentary's owners plan to keep a garden's entire yield from the poor; Deuteronomy says a forgotten sheaf must remain for the stranger, orphan, and widow, applying release to grain harvest.

row.basis: Ruth allowed to glean among the sheaves
row.note: The commentary's garden owners bar the poor from entering; Boaz tells his workers to let Ruth glean even among the sheaves and not reproach her, reversing exclusion in a concrete harvest scene.

row.basis: Extra grain deliberately left for Ruth
row.note: The commentary treats a crop's extract as a gift that may either flow or be retained; Boaz orders handfuls pulled from the bundles and left for Ruth, making generosity exceed mere permission to glean.

row.basis: A close relative as guardian and redeemer
row.note: The commentary says ancestry and kinship can be a refuge; Naomi identifies Boaz as a near kinsman and redeemer, where family connection becomes practical protection and provision.

row.basis: The day is short, work is abundant, and the master presses
row.note: The commentary calls late afternoon the point when work is nearly done and time for unfinished tasks narrows; this saying makes the same pressure explicit through a short day, much work, and an urgent master.

row.basis: An oath measures the time until oppression ends
row.note: The commentary opens with an oath on time and leaves the promised verdict just beyond the verse; Daniel's angel swears by the living God and gives a measured period whose end coincides with the breaking of the holy people's power.

row.basis: Blessed is the one who waits to the appointed days
row.note: The commentary includes delayed arrival, a fleeting moment, and patience through hard years; Daniel blesses the person who waits and reaches the stated number of days, linking endurance to a measured end.

row.basis: An oath that there will be no more delay
row.note: The commentary hears both a broad age and a late, shortened interval in asr; Revelation's angel swears that there will be no more delay before the mystery is completed, joining oath, waiting, and time's end.

row.basis: The oath is directed at the disobedient
row.note: The commentary places an oath before a verdict of loss; Hebrews continues its reading of Psalm 95 by identifying those excluded from rest as the disobedient, specifying why the sworn exclusion occurs.

row.basis: Unbelief prevents entry
row.note: The commentary moves from a general human loss to an exception for believers; Hebrews says the wilderness generation could not enter because of unbelief, giving the faith contrast a precise interpretive role.

row.basis: The present day is still called Today
row.note: The commentary treats a named time as a threshold before action becomes too late; Hebrews says God again appoints a day called Today and warns against hardening the heart, reading the old oath as a present opportunity.

row.basis: Prayer when heaven is shut and rain withheld
row.note: The commentary connects prayer at a set time with clouds, rain, and crop yield; Solomon prays for the people when heaven is closed and there is no rain, linking drought, prayer, repentance, and renewed provision.

row.basis: Arabic ع ص ر / Hebrew עצר; table sound correspondence, unverified
row.note: The package table marks Hebrew עצר as a possible sound correspondence to Arabic ع ص ر; Solomon's prayer describes heaven being shut so rain stops, a relevant restraint of the rain that the commentary links to yield, without proving cognacy.

row.basis: God is refuge in the cave prayer
row.note: The commentary treats a cave as refuge for people whose time is hidden from them; Psalm 142's superscription places David in a cave, and the cited verse calls God his refuge and portion while he is in distress.

row.basis: Fleeing for refuge and holding fast to hope
row.note: The commentary joins seeking shelter with clinging tightly to a person or place; Hebrews describes people who have fled for refuge to seize the hope set before them, bringing refuge and grasping together.

row.basis: Daniel prays three times each day under threat
row.note: The commentary describes believers praying at the day's edges; Daniel continues praying three times daily toward Jerusalem despite a decree that endangers his life, showing fixed prayer times maintained under pressure.

row.basis: The Lord's Prayer said three times daily
row.note: The commentary names the afternoon prayer and describes morning-evening devotion; the Didache directs Christians to pray the Lord's Prayer three times a day, evidence of a timed daily discipline.

row.basis: Cornelius prays at the ninth hour
row.note: The commentary leaves open the afternoon-prayer sense of asr; Acts places Cornelius in prayer at the ninth hour when he sees an angel, a distinct Christian scene of late-day devotion.

row.basis: Evening, midnight, cockcrow, and morning
row.note: The commentary lets one unqualified time-name span an afternoon, an era, or a fleeting interval; Jesus lists the night watches and warns that the master may come at any one of them, making readiness depend on an unknown hour.

row.basis: Prayer rises like incense
row.note: The commentary describes perfume swelling and rising behind a passing person; the psalm asks that prayer rise like incense, a distinct connection to the commentary's scent image apart from this verse's evening-offering detail.

row.basis: Wind releases garden spices and fruit
row.note: The commentary brings together wind, garden produce, and fragrance carried after movement; the Song calls on the winds to blow through a garden so its spices flow and its fruits can be eaten, joining those images in one scene.

row.basis: Fragrance set beside the day of death
row.note: The commentary follows a woman's perfume trail into a reflection on what remains after someone passes and also makes asr a life's closing time; Ecclesiastes says a good name is better than fragrant oil and the day of death better than birth.

row.basis: Sow in the morning and keep working in the evening
row.note: The commentary says the late day leaves little time for work still undone and connects time with uncertain yield; Ecclesiastes commands sowing in the morning and not letting the hand rest in the evening because the outcome is unknown.

row.basis: Light darkens as old age approaches
row.note: The commentary hears afternoon's fading light alongside the end of a human life; Ecclesiastes depicts sun, light, moon, and stars darkening as the days of aging arrive, giving that decline a bodily and cosmic image.

row.basis: A life poured out as departure nears
row.note: The commentary treats squeezing as extracting a life-giving essence and asr as the close of a lifespan; Paul says he is already being poured out as a libation and that the time of his departure has come.

row.basis: Transformation in a moment at the last trumpet
row.note: The commentary holds long ages beside the instant and says a whole lifetime can shrink to a small part of a day; Paul places the change of the dead in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet.

row.basis: A grain dies and bears much fruit
row.note: The commentary describes grain protected in its husk through scarcity and later used for food; Jesus says a grain of wheat must fall into the earth and die to bear much fruit, making fruitful release rather than protected storage the condition of abundance.

row.basis: Harvest comes in due time to those who do not give up
row.note: The commentary links the final patience-word to waiting through lean years for stored grain to yield; Paul urges continued good work because harvest comes at the proper time if one does not grow weary.

row.basis: The tested righteous are refined like gold
row.note: The commentary says time's pressure extracts an essence and connects patience with a bitter extract; Wisdom pictures the tested righteous as gold tried in a furnace and accepted like a burnt offering, interpreting pressure as refinement.

row.basis: A material gift is a fragrant offering
row.note: The commentary makes pressed yield an image of generosity and perfume a good trace left behind; Paul calls the Philippians' delivered gift a fragrant offering, joining concrete giving with lingering fragrance.

row.basis: The fragrance of knowledge spreads everywhere
row.note: The commentary describes a scent rising and trailing after movement; Paul says God spreads the fragrance of knowledge through the apostles everywhere, turning a passing procession into a lasting trail.

row.basis: Aroma received differently by the saved and perishing
row.note: The commentary contrasts a good trace left behind with destructive dust and loss; Paul says the same aroma is associated with those being saved and those perishing, adding opposed outcomes to the scent image.

row.basis: Bitter water becomes drinkable
row.note: The commentary's poem imagines water itself as the thing choking the speaker, with no rescuing sip left; at Marah, God shows Moses a tree and the bitter water becomes sweet, a contrasting scene where the obstructing water is made into relief.

row.basis: The gardener asks for one more year
row.note: The commentary's old garden owner loses his final yield when there is no time or strength to plant again; Jesus' gardener asks for another year to dig and fertilize the barren tree, making time an opportunity for restoration.

row.basis: Rich toward God rather than oneself
row.note: The commentary contrasts generous outflow with stored yield kept from others; Jesus concludes that the farmer who stores goods for himself is not rich toward God, giving the accumulation scene its ethical verdict.

row.basis: A fixed chasm makes relief impossible
row.note: The commentary's thirsty speaker has no remaining rescue sip; Abraham says a great chasm is fixed between the two places and no one can cross, explaining why the rich man's requested relief cannot arrive.

row.basis: Stored wealth decays
row.note: The commentary's pressed yield can leave only a dry remainder, and its garden owners lose what they tried to retain; James says riches have rotted and garments are moth-eaten, showing stored wealth failing to preserve its owner.

row.basis: Corroded treasure testifies in the last days
row.note: The commentary joins accumulation and the closing time of a life; James says hoarded gold and silver corrode and become evidence against their owners in the last days, making stored wealth a witness to judgment.

row.basis: Withheld wages cry out to God
row.note: The commentary describes a father withholding a child's property and garden owners denying the poor their produce; James says wages kept back from workers cry out, giving retention a concrete social and judicial consequence.

row.basis: Luxury before the day of slaughter
row.note: The commentary's aging garden owner loses the yield on which his future depends; James depicts the rich living in pleasure and fattening their hearts for a day of slaughter, joining abundance to an approaching end.
